questions.q: Why do networking engineers describe a network in layers rather than as one single process?
options: It is required by international law
Each layer does its own independent job and hands off to the layer above or below, so each can be built and troubleshot on its own
Layers make hardware cheaper to manufacture
It reduces the number of devices needed on a network
questions.explain: A layered model breaks the overall job into independent pieces. Each layer only needs to do its own job, which is why the application layer doesn't change even when the physical layer underneath it does.

questions.q: Which OSI layer uses IP addresses to deliver data across different networks?
questions.explain: The Network layer (OSI layer 3) handles delivery across different networks using IP addresses and routing.

questions.q: How does the TCP/IP model relate to the OSI model?
options: TCP/IP replaces OSI's Network layer only
TCP/IP collapses OSI's seven layers into four, combining Physical+Data Link into Network Access and Session+Presentation+Application into Application
OSI is used in production networks while TCP/IP is only theoretical
questions.explain: TCP/IP is the simpler four-layer model actually implemented in real hardware and software; it collapses OSI's seven layers by merging the bottom two into Network Access and the top three into Application.

questions.q: A Northbridge Retail register has link lights off on its network cable entirely. Which layer does this point to?
questions.explain: No link lights at all points to a problem with the cable or signal itself — the Physical layer, OSI layer 1.

questions.q: Which OSI layer is responsible for identifying which specific application on a device a packet is intended for, using port numbers?
questions.explain: The Transport layer uses TCP or UDP along with port numbers to deliver data to the correct application on a device, not just the correct device.
